sources.claim: Provider rule of thumb (OpenAI help article): for English text one token is about 4 characters or about three quarters of a word; exact counts depend on the model and its tokenizer. Token counts are not word counts.

sections.skill: Explain tokens and why counts differ from words

questions.prompt: What is a token?

choices.text: A chunk of text, such as a word or part of one
A coin you pay with to use an AI website
A password that unlocks a model
A whole page of text read at once

questions.correct_answer: A chunk of text, such as a word or part of one
questions.intro: Language models do not read words the way people do. They read and write TOKENS: chunks of text that may be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or a space. A common word like "the" is often one token, while a long or rare word like "unbelievably" may be split into several. For English, one provider's rule of thumb is about 4 characters, or about three quarters of a word, per token, but the exact count depends on the model. Token counts matter because limits on how much text a model can handle, and many usage prices, are measured in tokens, not words.

questions.prompt: About how many tokens is 30 words?
questions.intro: A simple estimate turns words into tokens. One provider's rule of thumb for English is that a token is about three quarters of a word. To estimate tokens from words, DIVIDE the number of words by 0.75, which is the same as multiplying by 4 and then dividing by 3. Example: 60 words / 0.75 = 80 tokens. To estimate words from tokens, MULTIPLY tokens by 0.75. Example: 200 tokens x 0.75 = 150 words. These are rough estimates for ordinary English, not exact counts.

sections.title: Apply it

questions.prompt: A message with a long table of numbers uses many more tokens than a story of the same word count. Why?

choices.text: Tables are always converted into images first
Numbers and table symbols often take more tokens
Numbers always count as zero tokens
Stories are never counted in tokens

questions.correct_answer: Numbers and table symbols often take more tokens
questions.intro: Token counts can surprise you. Text in some languages, unusual spellings, long numbers, code and tables often use more tokens per word than everyday English, so the same message length in words can cost more tokens. Because a model sees tokens rather than letters, tasks such as counting the letters in a word or reversing a word can trip it up even when it writes fluent sentences. And because different models split text differently, a count from one tool is only an estimate for another.
questions.feedback: Long numbers and symbols raise token counts.
